title: A number whose square is minus one

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the arrow from 0 to 1 turning a quarter turn to point straight up, j, and a second quarter turn landing it on −1, when you tap × j twice.
interactive.title: The quarter turn
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on one number line with an arrow from 0 to 1. A × −1 button swings the arrow round through the top to −1, drawn as a turn and never a flip, and pressing it again swings it on round to 1, a full turn. A turn handle sets any turn anticlockwise and draws it done twice, as a second dashed arrow. The smaller turn that done twice lands on −1 is the quarter turn, 90°, which leaves the arrow pointing straight up, off the line; that direction is j. Three quarter turns, 270°, done twice is 540°, a full turn and a half, so it lands on −1 too, with the arrow pointing straight down: that is −j. A × j button then steps the arrow a quarter turn anticlockwise each tap, 1, j, −1, −j, 1, with the power of j read out at each step. Later screens stretch the arrow to 3 before turning it, read √−9 as j3 and show the two views of how to start, from √−1 or from j × j = −1, and finish the quadratic x² + 2x + 5 = 0 with the quadratic formula. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, a wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? replays the turns for it.
interactive.ignores: The turns are animated over a moment so you can follow them, but multiplying takes no time: only where the arrow ends counts. Lengths are drawn to fit the screen. The name imaginary, which books give the j part, does not mean it is made up: later lessons measure j parts in ohms.

explain.text:
Multiplying by −1 turns a number's arrow half way round, so a quarter turn done twice does the same job as multiplying by −1. That quarter turn is a new number, j, and j × j = −1. A new number is needed because on the number line no number squares to a negative. 3 × 3 = 9, and as in Negative numbers, −3 × −3 = 9 too, while 0 × 0 = 0. So x² = −9 has no answer on the line. In Quadratics, a negative b² − 4ac meant no real roots, and x² + 2x + 5 = 0 is one of those, with b² − 4ac = 4 − 20 = −16.

Draw each number as an arrow from 0. Multiplying by −1 keeps the arrow's length and points it the other way, so 3 becomes −3: the arrow is turned through 180 degrees, a half turn.[^1] On the line a half turn and a mirror at 0 land in the same place, but a turn can be split into two equal smaller turns, and that smaller turn is what we are looking for. Multiply by −1 twice and the arrow makes a full turn, 360°, back where it started, which fits −1 × −1 = 1. Now look for a number that, multiplied in twice, does what −1 does. Its turn done twice must make a half turn. A quarter turn, 90°, does, and it leaves the arrow from 1 pointing straight up, off the line. No number on the line could do that, since none squares to a negative. So it is a new number, called [[j]]. Multiplying by j turns an arrow through +90 degrees, a quarter turn anticlockwise,[^2] and two quarter turns make a half turn, so j × j = −1.[^3] Three quarter turns, 270°, done twice make 540°, a full turn and a half, so they land on −1 as well. That turn leaves the arrow pointing straight down, and it is −j, so −j × −j = −1 too. Engineers write j where maths books write i,[^6] because i already means electric current.[^4]

Keep tapping × j and the arrow goes round: 1, j, −1, −j, 1. So j² = −1, j³ = j² × j = −j, and j⁴ = j² × j² = −1 × −1 = 1, and the powers repeat every four. Stretch the arrow to 3 first and (j3)² = j × j × 3 × 3 = −9, so j3 answers x² = −9, and so does −j3. Some books, mathcentre among them, start the other way: j stands for the square root of −1, and j² = −1 follows.[^3] One paper on teaching it calls that start unjustifiable, because it leads to misconceptions.[^7] This lesson leads with j × j = −1, because two numbers, j and −j, square to −1, and because the usual rule √a × √b = √(ab) breaks when both numbers are negative. People call j the square root of −1, and in the same way read √−4 as j2 and √−9 as j3, since (j3)² = −9: the rule would give √36 = 6, but j2 × j3 = j × j × 6 = −6. Back to the quadratic: −16 is (j4)², so the formula gives x = (−2 ± j4) ÷ 2 = −1 ± j2. Textbooks call a number like −1 + j2, an ordinary number plus a j part, a [[complex number]], written a + jb in general: −1 is its [[real part]] and 2 its j part, which books also call the imaginary part. The name does not mean made up: later lessons measure the j part of a circuit in ohms.

The course's puzzle turns on two currents out of step with the supply in opposite directions,[^5] and j is how later lessons write a quarter turn. **Multiplying by −1 is a half turn,[^1] so j, the quarter turn,[^2] done twice makes it: j × j = −1.[^3]**

analogy.text: In Trigonometry you drew an AC wave as a turning arrow. Shift a sine wave by half a cycle, 180°, and every value becomes its negative, the same as multiplying the wave by −1. A quarter-cycle shift, 90°, done twice is that half cycle, so the quarter-cycle shift plays the part of j.
analogy.breaks: A phase shift moves a whole wave along in time, while j turns one fixed arrow. And a sine wave shifted by 90° is not the old wave times any ordinary number, since its values do not rise and fall in step, which is the analogy's version of j being off the number line. Once the wave is drawn as its turning arrow, though, the analogy becomes exact: turning that arrow 90° is just what multiplying by j does, as lessons 5 to 8 use it.

practice.text:
- Treat j as a letter while you multiply, then put −1 wherever j × j appears.
- For a power of j, take out fours: each j⁴ is 1, so only what is left over counts. j⁶ = j⁴ × j² = −1.
- To solve x² = −9, or minus any positive number, the answers are j3 and −j3: j times the square root of the positive number, and its negative. Square each to check.
- In the quadratic formula, when b² − 4ac is negative, write it as a j number squared, as −16 = (j4)², then carry on.
- When both numbers under the square roots are negative, √a × √b = √(ab) gives the wrong sign. Write each one with j first.

**Rule of thumb:** Two js make a minus. If in doubt, count quarter turns anticlockwise: one is j, two is −1, three is −j, four is home.

**Worked example:** x² + 6x + 13 = 0. b² − 4ac = 36 − 52 = −16 = (j4)², so x = (−6 ± j4) ÷ 2 = −3 ± j2. Check −3 + j2: (−3 + j2)² = 9 − j12 + j × j × 4 = 5 − j12, then 6x = −18 + j12, and 5 − j12 − 18 + j12 + 13 = 0.

**Common mistakes**
- Taking j × j as +1, so j3 × j2 becomes 6. It is −6.
- Losing the sign on a power. j³ is j² × j = −j, not j and not −1.
- Giving one answer to x² = −9. j3 and −j3 both square to −9.
- Seeing × −1 as a mirror. On the line it lands in the same place, but a half turn splits into two equal quarter turns, and that quarter turn is j.
